players.product: 22/28nm and mature-node logic foundry; silicon interposers

quarterly_data.signal: CFO Chi-Tung Liu: Q2 2026 consolidated revenue was TWD 68.73 billion, up 12.6% quarter-over-quarter, with gross margin improving by over 3 percentage points to 32.5% (TWD 22.3 billion). Investment and dividend income together reached TWD 30 billion in non-operating income on recent stock market performance, lifting net income attributable to shareholders of the parent to TWD 42.26 billion and EPS to TWD 3.39. Utilization climbed to 85% from 79% in Q1; total wafer shipments reached 1.13 million 12-inch wafer equivalents (CEO: up 10.6% quarter-on-quarter, driven by strong demand in communications and consumer); blended ASP increased by a low single-digit percentage. First half 2026: revenue up 11.3% year-over-year to TWD 129.77 billion, gross margin up over 3 percentage points to 30.9% (TWD 40.1 billion), non-operating income TWD 35.6 billion, net income TWD 58.4 billion, EPS TWD 4.68. Cash on hand around TWD 124.7 billion; total equity TWD 443.9 billion at the end of Q2.
quarterly_data.figure: Q2 revenue TWD 68.73 billion (12.6% QoQ); GM 32.5%; net income TWD 42.26 billion; EPS TWD 3.39; utilization 85% (from 79%); 1.13 million 12-inch equivalent wafers (10.6% QoQ); 1H26 revenue TWD 129.77 billion (11.3% YoY)

quarterly_data.signal: Q2 2026 revenue mix (CFO): Asia remained the largest revenue pool at around 66% of total revenue and North America about 22%; IDM customers around 15% versus 14% in the previous quarter; almost no change across the three major application segments. Revenue below 40nm is still around 52%, with 22nm/28nm the largest revenue pool at 37% of total revenue. CEO Jason Wang: 22/28nm revenue continues to set record highs, with 22nm alone 17.5% of Q2 sales; the specialty offering, which includes power management, represents around 50% of revenue today.
quarterly_data.figure: Asia ~66%, North America ~22%; IDM ~15% (from 14%); below 40nm ~52%; 22nm/28nm 37%; 22nm 17.5%; specialty ~50% of revenue

quarterly_data.signal: Q3 2026 guidance (CEO Jason Wang): wafer shipments will increase by high single digits, driven by strong demand for power management ICs, sensors and microcontrollers, with demand momentum expected to remain stable across computer, communication and consumer; ASP in US dollars will remain firm; gross margin in the mid-30% range; capacity utilization greater than 90%. CFO: the higher Q3 gross margin guidance is mainly attributed to the higher utilization rate (85% in Q2, above 90% guided for Q3). CEO: UMC's full-year 2026 wafer shipments will grow year-on-year on 22/28nm and 8-inch, driven by foundry share gains and customer share gains in both AI and non-AI markets, even as consumer (handset, PC, notebook) declines year-over-year.
quarterly_data.figure: Q3 wafer shipments up high single digits; ASP firm in USD; GM mid-30% range; utilization greater than 90%

quarterly_data.signal: Capacity and loading (CEO / CFO): quarterly capacity at the Singapore site Fab 12i showed some increase in Q2, with a more meaningful increase in the coming quarter to reach 192,000 12-inch wafer capacity for the Singapore site. 12-inch capacity is already at a healthy utilization rate and still above the corporate average, and mature 12-inch loading will rise quarter-on-quarter on AI-related demand; the 8-inch portfolio is seeing a strong rebound, with 8-inch loading improving significantly in Q3 to the mid-80% range.
quarterly_data.figure: Singapore (Fab 12i) capacity to reach 192,000 12-inch wafers next quarter; 8-inch loading to mid-80% range in Q3

quarterly_data.signal: Capex raised and expansion approved: the Board approved a plan to expand cleanroom capacity at the Singapore P4 facility and to construct a new fab in Tainan, Taiwan, executed in phases with facility deployment paced to customer demand (CEO: every phase based on market validation, alignment and customer commitment). The 2026 capex budget is raised to USD 2 billion from USD 1.5 billion to support growing customer demand in silicon photonics and advanced packaging. CFO: the Board approved nearly USD 5 billion of capex over the next two to three years - USD 5 billion to be spent across 2026 and 2027, with 2028 to be determined by future phase decisions. Singapore P4 gets a cleanroom and equipment to expand silicon photonics capacity; in Tainan, construction of 12A P7 and P8 (foundation shells) will let UMC scale advanced packaging, with P7 prepared for advanced packaging. CEO: construction lead times are roughly greater than 20 months, putting meaningful capacity in the 2028-2029 timeframe; detailed schedules will follow once equipment installers and contractors confirm.
quarterly_data.figure: 2026 capex USD 2 billion (from USD 1.5 billion); Board-approved nearly USD 5 billion across 2026 and 2027; lead times greater than 20 months, meaningful capacity 2028-2029

quarterly_data.signal: Capacity additions inside existing facilities (CEO Jason Wang): part of the approved capex includes capacity expansion in the P3 facility, and in existing facilities UMC will add BCD (power management solutions) as well as silicon photonics; in Taiwan 12A UMC will start putting in CMS (customized memory stacking) and DTC solutions; test capacity is being set up in the 8-inch facilities. Given tooling and install time, some production ramps are expected in late 2027 to early 2028.
quarterly_data.figure: production ramps expected late 2027 to early 2028

quarterly_data.signal: CFO Chi-Tung Liu on margins: new projects such as silicon photonics and advanced packaging are expected to enhance EBITDA margin, but the new Tainan fab and Singapore cleanroom will raise depreciation, offsetting gross margin. Depreciation is now expected to increase by low teens year-over-year for at least 2026 and 2027 (the new cleanroom and shells change the curve); 2028 depends on capex. Over the next two to three years EBITDA margin is expected to improve steadily; the focus is higher profit in absolute dollars, with gross margin dependent on how depreciation is booked.
quarterly_data.figure: depreciation to rise low teens year-over-year in 2026 and 2027

quarterly_data.signal: AI-related revenue (CEO Jason Wang): UMC's AI-related business is driven by specialty solutions - power management, connectivity, FPGA - plus the growing advanced packaging and silicon photonics business, and has begun to become an important contributor to growth in 2026. AI-related revenue is projected to be close to approximately USD 300 million this year, and UMC expects it to exceed USD 1 billion in three years. Silicon photonics and advanced packaging, still at an early stage, have the highest CAGR; connectivity and power management are major contributors. In the near term UMC sees upside in silicon photonics, power and FPGA-related products, particularly in 40nm and 65nm technologies.
quarterly_data.figure: AI-related revenue close to approximately USD 300 million in 2026; expected to exceed USD 1 billion in three years

quarterly_data.signal: Silicon photonics (CEO Jason Wang): earlier this month UMC announced its first mass production delivery of a 12-inch photonics IC to a customer, which it calls a major milestone demonstrating high-volume silicon photonics manufacturing on 12-inch wafers; the silicon photonics platform is to be available for general customer use in 2027. UMC says it is the first to offer a 12-inch solution, with better process control and performance than 8-inch competitors (lower propagation loss and better yield, demonstrated to customers). In TFLN, UMC says it has the world's first TFLN modulator in production and is developing 40G per lane and beyond, supporting beyond-400G use cases. TFLN components can be combined with UMC's silicon photonics PICs through advanced packaging: UMC can offer optical I/O interposers with PICs and provide TFLN components for CPO solutions.
quarterly_data.figure: first mass-production delivery of a 12-inch photonics IC; platform general availability 2027; TFLN 40G per lane in development, beyond 400G

quarterly_data.signal: Advanced packaging (CEO Jason Wang): UMC started with interposer solutions and RF SOI 3D IC and chiplet solutions and now offers more, and projects its addressable market to more than double by 2030 as it expands from 2.5D interposers with DTC and discrete DTC to wafer-to-wafer stacking and memory-to-memory stacking. More than ten active customers and over 35 new products are in discussion, with expected tape-outs in 2026 and early 2027; a high percentage of those products are DTC, which is a significant portion. UMC has entered production for 3D wafer-to-wafer hybrid bonding, bridge die and discrete DTC. It is not positioning as a direct CoWoS alternative, and works across the entire ecosystem rather than with a single partner. CEO: 'We believe we are ahead of our peers in advanced packaging, which is leading to share gains and many new opportunities.'
quarterly_data.figure: addressable market to more than double by 2030; more than ten active customers; over 35 new products in discussion; tape-outs 2026 and early 2027

quarterly_data.signal: Intel 12nm cooperation (CEO Jason Wang): the 12nm project with Intel is advancing smoothly; the PDK will be ready in May 2026 and customer design-ins are expected to be ready to tape out in 2027, so 2027 is still an early pilot ramp stage and production will probably be more meaningful in 2028. The business model will be accretive to current financials as it ramps, with most meaningful revenue as volume ramps in 2028 and beyond. The 12nm is being extended to high-voltage derivatives (essentially 14nm-equivalent high-voltage variants). CEO / CFO: UMC must first deliver and commercialize 12nm before deciding on nodes beyond it; the current focus is on 12nm only.
quarterly_data.figure: 12nm PDK ready May 2026; tape-outs 2027; meaningful volume 2028 and beyond

quarterly_data.signal: CEO Jason Wang on demand: worldwide demand is improving with broader, more sustainable momentum but remains AI-led, spilling into memory, connectivity and power; AI-related demand remains very strong and XPU demand strong, and the bottleneck is not only compute but also memory, connectivity and power management. Non-AI demand is uneven - not yet a full-blown broad-based recovery - and consumer (handset, PC, notebook) will decline year-over-year. Supply reduction plus inventory normalization are giving more visibility. The CEO sees this cycle as different from the previous broad-based one, with AI the primary growth driver.

Customer inventory (CEO Jason Wang): cautious but not alarmed. In Q1 2026 days of inventory rose slightly - partly early stocking in HPC due to rising memory prices; smartphone and consumer inventories are rising, indicating end-market weakness; automotive and industrial demand is stable but DOI remains above historical averages. For Q2 2026, with semiconductor sales expected to stay strong in 2026, DOI is expected to rise by several days again.

Pricing (CEO Jason Wang): UMC keeps value-based pricing rather than maximizing short-term pricing on the cycle. As industry conditions improve the pricing environment is becoming more constructive; customer engagements are constructive given improved visibility, and UMC expects annual pricing trends to be better than it had anticipated, with more meaningful pricing uplift in 2027.
quarterly_data.figure: more meaningful pricing uplift expected in 2027
